```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4, warning = FALSE)
library(amorem)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 0), "%")
chg <- function(from, to) if (to > from) "raises" else "lowers"
```

# Hyperedge models

`amorem` supports **relational hyper event models** (RHEMs), the extension of
REMs from dyadic `(sender, receiver, time)` events to set-valued
`(I, J, time)` hyperedges, where `I` is a set of senders and `J` is a set of
receivers. Following
[Boschi, Lerner & Wit (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05289), a single
event can involve several actors per axis: a paper authored by a co-author set
citing a set of references, an e-mail sent to several recipients at once, or a
multi-actor meeting (`J = ∅`). The code on this page runs when the page is
built.

---

## Data model

```{r data-model}
hl <- hyperedge_log(
  I    = list(c("alice", "bob"), c("alice", "carol"), c("bob", "carol")),
  J    = list(c("paperA"),        c("paperA", "paperB"), c("paperB")),
  time = c(1.0, 2.5, 4.0))

is_hyperedge_log(hl)
hyperedge_sizes(hl)
```

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `hyperedge_log(I, J, time)` | Validating constructor; sorts by time |
| `is_hyperedge_log(x)` | Structural predicate |
| `as_hyperedge_log(event_log)` | Promote a dyadic log (each row becomes a singleton on each axis) |
| `as_dyadic_log(h)` | Inverse; succeeds only when `|I| = |J| = 1` on every row |
| `hyperedge_sizes(h)` | Adds `size_I` and `size_J` columns |

A dyadic log and its hyperedge form convert into each other:

```{r round-trip}
dy <- data.frame(sender = c("a", "b"), receiver = c("b", "c"), time = c(1, 2))
h  <- as_hyperedge_log(dy)
h$I
as_dyadic_log(h)
try(as_dyadic_log(hl))   # rows with two senders are not dyadic
```

For **undirected hyperevents** (e.g. multi-actor meetings), pass
`J = list(character(0), ...)` and use the actor-only simulator below.

---

## Subset repetition

The hyperedge-native covariates of the paper (eq. 3-4) count how often parts
of a focal hyperedge have occurred together before time `t`:

```{r subrep}
# past events containing both {alice, bob} and {paperA}
hyperedge_activity(hl, I = c("alice", "bob"), J = "paperA", t = 5)

# share-weighted repetition over the size-2 subsets of I, paired with paperA
hyperedge_subrep(hl, I = c("alice", "bob", "carol"), J = "paperA",
                 t = 5, rho = 2, l = 1)
```

`hyperedge_subrep(rho, l)` averages, over all sender subsets of size `rho` and
receiver subsets of size `l`, the number of past events that contain both
subsets. For dyadic events with `|I| = |J| = 1`, `rho = 1, l = 1` is the count
of past events on the same dyad.

### Feature engine

`hyperedge_features()` is the hyperedge analogue of `endogenous_features()`.
It evaluates each statistic at every row of the log, using the events strictly
before that row:

```{r features}
hyperedge_features(hl, stats = c("activity", "subrep_1_1", "subrep_2_1"))
```

| Stat name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"activity"` | `hyperedge_activity()` on each row's `(I, J)` |
| `"subrep_<rho>_<l>"` | directed subset repetition (`NA` when the row has fewer than `rho` senders or `l` receivers) |
| `"subrep_<rho>"` | undirected subset repetition (`l = 0`) |
| a name from the dyadic catalogue | delegated to `endogenous_features()` after `as_dyadic_log()`; requires every row to be dyadic |

---

## Case study · multi-recipient e-mail

In `radoslaw_email` (internal e-mail of a manufacturing company), an e-mail
sent to several recipients appears as one row per recipient with the same
sender and time stamp. Grouping the rows by sender and time gives a directed
hyperevent: `I = {sender}`, `J = {recipients}`. We use the first 7 days.

```{r email-log}
data(radoslaw_email)
x <- radoslaw_email[radoslaw_email$time < 7 &
                    radoslaw_email$sender != radoslaw_email$receiver, ]
key <- paste(x$sender, x$time)
first <- !duplicated(key)
J_sets <- lapply(split(as.character(x$receiver),
                       factor(key, levels = unique(key))), unique)
email_hl <- hyperedge_log(I = as.list(as.character(x$sender[first])),
                          J = unname(J_sets), time = x$time[first])
email_hl <- hyperedge_sizes(email_hl)
c(rows = nrow(x), hyperevents = nrow(email_hl),
  multi_recipient = sum(email_hl$size_J > 1),
  actors = length(unique(c(x$sender, x$receiver))))
```

```{r email-numbers, include = FALSE}
n_multi <- sum(email_hl$size_J > 1)
share_rows_multi <- sum(email_hl$size_J[email_hl$size_J > 1]) / nrow(x)
```

```{r email-sizes, fig.alt = "Distribution of recipient-set sizes and of e-mails per sender"}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
tab <- table(pmin(email_hl$size_J, 11))
names(tab)[names(tab) == "11"] <- "11+"
barplot(tab, log = "y", col = "#5b9bd5", xlab = "recipients per e-mail",
        ylab = "e-mails (log scale)", main = "recipient-set size",
        ylim = c(1, 2 * max(tab)), cex.names = 0.6)
per_sender <- sort(table(unlist(email_hl$I)), decreasing = TRUE)
plot(seq_along(per_sender), as.numeric(per_sender), log = "y", type = "h",
     col = "#1d4e89", xlab = "sender rank", ylab = "e-mails (log scale)",
     main = "e-mails per sender")
par(op)
```

Of the `r fmt(nrow(email_hl), 0)` e-mails, `r fmt(n_multi, 0)`
(`r pct(n_multi / nrow(email_hl))`) have more than one recipient; they account
for `r pct(share_rows_multi)` of the `r fmt(nrow(x), 0)` rows of the dyadic
log. The largest recipient set has `r max(email_hl$size_J)` members.

The single-recipient e-mails form an ordinary dyadic log again, so the dyadic
catalogue applies to them directly:

```{r email-dyadic}
single <- email_hl[email_hl$size_J == 1, c("I", "J", "time")]
class(single) <- class(email_hl)
dy_single <- as_dyadic_log(single)
head(endogenous_features(dy_single, stats = c("reciprocity_count", "recency")), 3)
```

### A size-matched case-control fit

`amorem` does not yet sample non-events for hyperevents, so the case-control
design is built here by hand: for each e-mail, one control hyperedge with the
same number of recipients, a sender drawn uniformly from the actors and a
recipient set drawn uniformly from the other actors (matching on cardinality,
as in Section 3.3 of the paper). Three statistics are evaluated for the event
and the control at the event's time, from the e-mails strictly before it:

- **sender activity**: past e-mails from the sender (`hyperedge_subrep(rho = 1, l = 0)`);
- **repetition**: past e-mails from the sender to each recipient, averaged over
  the recipients (`hyperedge_subrep(rho = 1, l = 1)`);
- **reciprocity**: past e-mails from each recipient to the sender, averaged over
  the recipients (`hyperedge_activity()` with the roles swapped).

```{r email-cc}
hstats <- function(I, J, t) c(
  sender_activity = hyperedge_subrep(email_hl, I, J, t, rho = 1, l = 0),
  repetition      = hyperedge_subrep(email_hl, I, J, t, rho = 1, l = 1),
  reciprocity     = mean(vapply(J, function(j)
                      hyperedge_activity(email_hl, I = j, J = I, t = t), 0)))

set.seed(11)
actors <- sort(unique(c(unlist(email_hl$I), unlist(email_hl$J))))
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(email_hl)), function(i) {
  I <- email_hl$I[[i]]; J <- email_hl$J[[i]]; t <- email_hl$time[i]
  s_c <- sample(actors, 1)
  J_c <- sample(setdiff(actors, s_c), length(J))
  rbind(data.frame(stratum = i, event = 1L, t(hstats(I, J, t))),
        data.frame(stratum = i, event = 0L, t(hstats(s_c, J_c, t))))
})
cc <- do.call(rbind, rows)
for (v in c("sender_activity", "repetition", "reciprocity"))
  cc[[paste0("log_", v)]] <- log1p(cc[[v]])

w <- widen_case_control(cc, covariates = c("log_sender_activity",
                                           "log_repetition", "log_reciprocity"))
fit <- rem(~ log_sender_activity + log_repetition + log_reciprocity,
           data = w, method = "gam")
est <- summary(fit)$p.table[, c("Estimate", "Std. Error")]
round(est, 3)
```

```{r email-cc-numbers, include = FALSE}
b <- est[, "Estimate"]; se <- est[, "Std. Error"]
```

All three statistics enter on the `log(1 + count)` scale. Holding the other two
fixed, the log-rate of an e-mail changes by `r fmt(b[["log_sender_activity"]])`
(standard error `r fmt(se[["log_sender_activity"]])`) per unit of sender
activity, by `r fmt(b[["log_repetition"]])` (s.e.
`r fmt(se[["log_repetition"]])`) per unit of repetition and by
`r fmt(b[["log_reciprocity"]])` (s.e. `r fmt(se[["log_reciprocity"]])`) per
unit of reciprocity. A control
is drawn from all actor sets of the same size, so these coefficients compare
each e-mail with an arbitrary hyperedge of its size; a design that also matches
on the sender would isolate the recipient-side effects.

---

## Two-mode directed simulator

For citation-style data (Boschi et al. 2025 Section 5),
`simulate_directed_hyperedge_events()` draws sender and receiver sets from two
actor pools. Supported endogenous statistics: `"size_I"`, `"size_J"`,
`"activity"`, `"subrep_<rho>_<l>"`. A 150-event sweep on 4 senders × 4
receivers, varying the endogenous terms one at a time:

```{r directed-sweep}
specs <- list(
  "no effect"         = c(),
  "size_I = -0.6"     = c(size_I = -0.6),
  "subrep_1_1 = 0.8"  = c(subrep_1_1 = 0.8),
  "both"              = c(size_I = -0.6, subrep_1_1 = 0.8))
sims <- lapply(specs, function(eff) {
  set.seed(2)
  simulate_directed_hyperedge_events(
    n_events = 150, senders = paste0("author", 1:4),
    receivers = paste0("paper", 1:4), max_size_I = 3, max_size_J = 3,
    baseline_rate = 0.3,
    endogenous_stats = if (length(eff)) names(eff) else NULL,
    endogenous_effects = if (length(eff)) eff else NULL)
})
sizes <- lapply(sims, hyperedge_sizes)
sweep <- data.frame(
  mean_size_I = vapply(sizes, function(s) mean(s$size_I), 0),
  mean_size_J = vapply(sizes, function(s) mean(s$size_J), 0),
  share_I_1   = vapply(sizes, function(s) mean(s$size_I == 1), 0))
round(sweep, 2)
```

```{r directed-figure, fig.alt = "Sender-set size distribution under the four specifications"}
counts <- sapply(sizes, function(s) table(factor(s$size_I, levels = 1:3)))
barplot(counts, beside = TRUE, col = c("#1d4e89", "#5b9bd5", "#bcd4ec"),
        ylab = "events", xlab = "specification",
        legend.text = paste("|I| =", 1:3),
        args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"))
```

With no endogenous effect, `r pct(sweep["no effect", "share_I_1"])` of the
events have a single sender. A negative `size_I` effect
`r chg(sweep["no effect", "share_I_1"], sweep["size_I = -0.6", "share_I_1"])`
that share to `r pct(sweep["size_I = -0.6", "share_I_1"])`; a positive
`subrep_1_1` effect
`r chg(sweep["no effect", "share_I_1"], sweep["subrep_1_1 = 0.8", "share_I_1"])`
it to `r pct(sweep["subrep_1_1 = 0.8", "share_I_1"])`, since it reinforces the
sender-receiver pairs that have already occurred; both effects together give
`r pct(sweep["both", "share_I_1"])`.

The simulator enumerates every candidate `(I, J)` for every event, so the cost
per event grows exponentially with the actor pools; it is practical for small
universes (about 10 actors per side, `max_size ≤ 3`).

---

## Undirected meeting simulator

For undirected multi-actor meetings (Section 4 of the paper),
`simulate_hyperedge_events()` enumerates every subset of `actors` of size
`min_size..max_size`, scores each from the event history, draws an event
proportional to its exponentiated score, and waits an exponential time with
rate equal to the total score. The output is a hyperedge log with empty
receiver sets.

```{r meetings}
set.seed(5)
meet <- simulate_hyperedge_events(
  n_events           = 150,
  actors             = LETTERS[1:5],
  max_size           = 3,
  baseline_rate      = 0.3,
  endogenous_stats   = c("subrep_2", "size"),
  endogenous_effects = c(subrep_2 = 0.6, size = -0.3))
pairs <- utils::combn(LETTERS[1:5], 2, simplify = FALSE)
pair_counts <- vapply(pairs, function(p)
  hyperedge_activity(meet, I = p, t = Inf), 0)
names(pair_counts) <- vapply(pairs, paste, "", collapse = "")
top <- names(which.max(pair_counts))
sort(pair_counts, decreasing = TRUE)[1:4]
```

```{r meetings-figure, fig.alt = "Running co-attendance count of the most frequent pair and of another pair"}
other <- names(sort(pair_counts))[1]
running <- function(p) cumsum(vapply(meet$I, function(Im)
  all(strsplit(p, "")[[1]] %in% Im), logical(1)))
label <- function(p) paste0("{", paste(strsplit(p, "")[[1]], collapse = ", "), "}")
plot(seq_len(nrow(meet)), running(top), type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "#d62728",
     xlab = "meeting index", ylab = "meetings containing the pair so far",
     ylim = c(0, max(pair_counts)))
lines(seq_len(nrow(meet)), running(other), type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "#1d4e89")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("#d62728", "#1d4e89"),
       legend = c(label(top), label(other)))
```

With `subrep_2 = 0.6`, a pair that meets is more likely to meet again. Of the
`r nrow(meet)` meetings, `r pair_counts[[top]]` contain the pair
{`r paste(strsplit(top, "")[[1]], collapse = ", ")`}, and
`r pair_counts[[other]]` contain the pair
{`r paste(strsplit(other, "")[[1]], collapse = ", ")`}.

## Time-varying and non-linear effects on hyperevents

`simulate_directed_hyperevents_tvnl()` simulates directed hyperevents between
groups of senders and groups of receivers, where a group's covariate is the
mean of its members' attributes. The sender-group covariate has a
time-varying effect \(\alpha(t)\) and the receiver-group covariate a
non-linear effect \(f(x)\). It returns a case-control table, which
`widen_case_control()` and `rem()` fit with `tv()` and `nl()` terms:

```{r tvnl}
set.seed(1234)
sa <- setNames(rnorm(4, 5, 1.5), paste0("S", 1:4))
ra <- setNames(rnorm(4, 3, 2.0), paste0("R", 1:4))
d  <- simulate_directed_hyperevents_tvnl(sa, ra, horizon = 4, n_controls = 1)
table(d$event)
wd <- widen_case_control(d, stratum = "event_id",
                         covariates = c("cov_sender", "cov_receiver", "event_time"))
fit_tvnl <- rem(~ tv(cov_sender, k = 6) + nl(cov_receiver, k = 6),
                data = wd, method = "gam", time = "event_time")
```

```{r tvnl-figure, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Estimated time-varying and non-linear effects against the truth"}
truth <- attr(d, "truth")
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
plot(fit_tvnl$fit, select = 1, rug = FALSE, scale = 0,
     xlab = "time", ylab = expression(alpha(t)), main = "time-varying effect")
tg <- seq(0, truth$horizon, length.out = 200)
lines(tg, truth$time_varying_effect(tg), col = "#d62728", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
plot(fit_tvnl$fit, select = 2, rug = FALSE, scale = 0,
     xlab = "receiver-group covariate", ylab = "f(x)", main = "non-linear effect")
xg <- seq(min(d$cov_receiver), max(d$cov_receiver), length.out = 200)
fx <- truth$nonlinear_effect(xg)
lines(xg, fx - mean(fx), col = "#d62728", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
par(op)
```

Solid lines are the estimates with ±2 standard-error bands, dashed red lines
the true effects; the non-linear effect is identified up to an additive
constant, so its truth is drawn centred.

---

## Smooth effects on hyperedge features

Once features are computed on a case-control table, linear, `tv()`, `nl()` and
`tvnl()` specifications are fitted with `rem()` as for dyadic data — see
[Estimation](estimation.html). The case-control likelihood is equation 8 of
Boschi et al. (2025).
